english: There is a code of manners, she knew, and its seventh article (possibly) states that on occasions like this one it falls to the woman, whatever her own work may be, to come to the aid of the young man across from her, so that he can bring out and relieve the thighbones and ribs of his vanity, his pressing need to assert himself. Just as it is men’s duty, she thought, with her old-maidish sense of fair play, to help us if, for instance, the Underground caught fire. In that case, she thought, I’d certainly expect Mr. Tansley to get me out. But what if, she wondered, neither of us did either? So she sat there, smiling.

english: “But how long do they keep men on a Lighthouse?” she asked. He told her; he was amazingly well informed. And because he was grateful, and he liked her, and he was starting to have a good time, Mrs. Ramsay thought that now she could slip back into that dreamland, that unreal but fascinating place—the Mannings’ drawing room at Marlow twenty years ago—where you moved about unhurried and untroubled, because there was no future to fret about. She knew what had become of them, and of herself. It was like rereading a good book, because she knew how that story ended—it had all happened twenty years ago—and life, which came spilling in cascades even off this dining table, heaven knows where to, was sealed up there, lying calm between its banks like a lake. He had said they’d built a billiard room—could it be true? Would William keep talking about the Mannings? She wanted him to. But no—for some reason the mood had left him. She tried, and he didn’t respond. She couldn’t make him. She felt let down.
danish_before_fix: »Men hvor længe beholder de folk på et fyr?« spurgte hun. Han fortalte det; han var forbløffende godt informeret. Og fordi han var taknemmelig, og han kunne lide hende, og han var begyndt at more sig, tænkte fru Ramsay, at nu kunne hun glide tilbage til det drømmeland, det uvirkelige men fascinerende sted — Mannings dagligstue i Marlow for tyve år siden — hvor man bevægede sig omkring uhastet og uanfægtet, fordi der ingen fremtid var at bekymre sig om. Hun vidste, hvad der var blevet af dem, og af hende selv. Det var som at genlæse en god bog, fordi hun vidste, hvordan den historie endte — det hele var sket for tyve år siden — og livet, som kom væltende i vandfald selv fra dette middagsbord, Gud ved hvorhen, var forseglet derovre og lå roligt mellem sine bredder som en sø. Han havde sagt, at de havde bygget et billardværelse — kunne det være sandt? Ville William blive ved med at tale om Mannings? Hun ønskede, at han ville. Men nej — af en eller anden grund havde stemningen forladt ham. Hun prøvede, og han reagerede ikke. Hun kunne ikke få ham til det. Hun følte sig svigtet.

english: “Andrew,” she said, “hold your plate lower, or I’ll spill it.” (The Bœuf en Daube was a complete triumph.) Here, she felt, laying down the spoon, was the still space around the heart of things, where you could move about or rest. She could wait now (everyone had been served), and listen; and then, like a hawk that suddenly drops from its height, she could flaunt and sink easily into laughter, leaning her whole weight on what her husband, at the far end of the table, was saying about the square root of one thousand two hundred and fifty-three, which happened to be the number on his train ticket.
danish_before_fix: »Andrew,« sagde hun, »hold din tallerken lavere, ellers spilder jeg.« (Bœuf en Daube var en fuldstændig triumf.) Her, følte hun, mens hun lagde skeen fra sig, var det stille rum omkring tingenes hjerte, hvor man kunne bevæge sig omkring eller hvile. Hun kunne vente nu (alle var blevet serveret) og lytte; og så, som en høg, der pludselig stryger ned fra sin højde, kunne hun hovere og synke let ned i latter, mens hun lænede hele sin vægt på det, hendes mand, for enden af bordet, sagde om kvadratroden af et tusinde to hundrede og treoghalvtreds, som tilfældigvis var nummeret på hans jernbanebillet.

english: “Let’s enjoy what we enjoy,” he said. To Mrs. Ramsay his integrity seemed altogether admirable. Not for a moment did he seem to think, But what does this mean for me? But if your temperament was the other kind, the kind that needs praise and needs encouragement, then of course you started (and she knew Mr. Ramsay was starting) to grow uneasy, to want someone to say, Oh, but your work will last, Mr. Ramsay, or something of the sort. He made his uneasiness plain enough now, remarking with some irritation that Scott (or was it Shakespeare?) would see him through his lifetime, anyway. He said it irritably. Everyone, she thought, felt slightly uncomfortable, without knowing why. Then Minta Doyle, who had good instincts, declared bluntly and absurdly that she didn’t believe anybody truly enjoyed reading Shakespeare. Very few people, Mr. Ramsay said grimly (though his mind had turned away again), liked it as much as they claimed. Still, he added, some of the plays have considerable merit, and Mrs. Ramsay saw that for now, at least, all would be well. He would laugh at Minta; and Minta, Mrs. Ramsay saw, sensing how intensely anxious he was about himself, would make sure in her own way that he was looked after, and would praise him somehow. But she wished it weren’t necessary; perhaps it was her own fault that it was. In any case, she was free now to listen to Paul Rayley, who was trying to say something about the books you read as a boy. Those lasted, he said. At school he had read some Tolstoy. There was one he never forgot, though he couldn’t remember what it was called. Russian names were impossible, said Mrs. Ramsay. “Vronsky,” said Paul. He remembered that one because he had always thought it made such a good name for a villain. “Vronsky,” Mrs. Ramsay said. “Oh, _Anna Karenina_.” But that did not get them much further; books were not really their line. No—Charles Tansley could correct them both about books in a moment, but with him it was all so tangled up with Am I saying the right thing? Am I making a good impression? that in the end you found out more about him than about Tolstoy. What Paul said, on the other hand, was simply about the thing itself, not about him. Like all stupid people he had a sort of modesty as well, a thought for what you were feeling, and every so often, at least, she found that attractive. At this moment he was thinking neither about himself nor about Tolstoy, but whether she was cold, whether there was a draft on her, whether she would like a pear.
danish_before_fix: »Lad os nyde det, vi nyder,« sagde han. For fru Ramsay forekom hans retskaffenhed helt beundringsværdig. Ikke et øjeblik syntes han at tænke, Men hvad betyder dette for mig? Men hvis ens temperament var af den anden slags, den slags, der har brug for ros og opmuntring, så begyndte man naturligvis (og hun vidste, at hr. Ramsay begyndte) at blive urolig, at ville have nogen til at sige, Åh, men Deres værk vil vare, hr. Ramsay, eller noget i den retning. Han gjorde sin uro tydelig nok nu, idet han med nogen irritation bemærkede, at Scott (eller var det Shakespeare?) i hvert fald ville række ham gennem hans levetid. Han sagde det irriteret. Alle, tænkte hun, følte sig lidt utilpas uden at vide hvorfor. Så erklærede Minta Doyle, der havde gode instinkter, ligeud og absurd, at hun ikke troede, nogen virkelig nød at læse Shakespeare. Meget få mennesker, sagde hr. Ramsay dystert (skønt hans tanker var vendt bort igen), kunne lide ham så meget, som de påstod. Alligevel, tilføjede han, har nogle af stykkerne betydelig værdi, og fru Ramsay så, at for nu, i det mindste, ville alt gå godt. Han ville le ad Minta; og Minta, så fru Ramsay, ville, idet hun fornemmede, hvor intenst bekymret han var for sig selv, på sin egen måde sørge for, at der blev taget vare på ham, og ville rose ham på en eller anden måde. Men hun ønskede, at det ikke var nødvendigt; måske var det hendes egen skyld, at det var. Under alle omstændigheder var hun fri nu til at lytte til Paul Rayley, som forsøgte at sige noget om de bøger, man læser som dreng. De varede, sagde han. I skolen havde han læst noget Tolstoj. Der var én, han aldrig glemte, skønt han ikke kunne huske, hvad den hed. Russiske navne var umulige, sagde fru Ramsay. »Vronskij,« sagde Paul. Han huskede den, fordi han altid havde syntes, det var et så godt navn til en skurk. »Vronskij,« sagde fru Ramsay. »Åh, _Anna Karenina_.« Men det bragte dem ikke ret meget længere; bøger var ikke rigtig deres område. Nej — Charles Tansley kunne rette dem begge om bøger i et nu, men hos ham var det hele så sammenfiltret med Siger jeg det rigtige? Gør jeg et godt indtryk? at man til sidst fandt mere ud af ham end af Tolstoj. Hvad Paul sagde, derimod, var blot om selve tingen, ikke om ham. Som alle dumme mennesker havde han også en slags beskedenhed, en tanke for, hvad man følte, og hver gang i mellem, i det mindste, fandt hun det tiltalende. I dette øjeblik tænkte han hverken på sig selv eller på Tolstoj, men på, om hun frøs, om der var gennemtræk, om hun ville have en pære.

english: she read, and turned the page, and swung herself, zigzagging here and there, from line to line as if from branch to branch, from one red and white flower to the next, until she was roused by a small sound—her husband slapping his thighs. For a second their eyes met; but neither wanted to talk. There was nothing to say, and still something seemed to pass between them, from him to her. It was the life of the book, its power, its enormous humor, she knew, that made him slap his thighs. Don’t interrupt, he seemed to be telling her; don’t speak; just sit. And he read on. His lips twitched. It filled him up. It gave him strength. All the petty irritations and jabs of the evening went clean out of his head—how unbearably dull he found it to sit still while people went on eating and drinking forever, how snappish he had been with his wife, how thin-skinned, how he had minded when they skipped over his books as if they did not exist. But now, he felt, it didn’t matter a damn who got to Z (if thought ran like an alphabet from A to Z). Someone would get there—if not he, then another man. The strength and sanity of this writer, his feeling for plain and simple things, these fishermen, the poor crazed old creature in Mucklebackit’s cottage (all in Scott’s _The Antiquary_), made him feel so full of vigor, so freed of something, that he was stirred and triumphant and could not choke back his tears. Lifting the book slightly to hide his face, he let the tears fall, and shook his head from side to side, and lost himself entirely (apart from one or two thoughts about morality, and French novels versus English ones, and how Scott’s hands were tied, though his view was perhaps as true as the other one)—lost all his own worries and failures in poor Steenie’s drowning and Mucklebackit’s grief (that was Scott at his finest) and in the astonishing pleasure and energy it gave him.

I et sekund mødtes deres øjne; men ingen af dem ville tale. Der var intet at sige, og alligevel syntes noget at gå mellem dem, fra ham til hende. Det var bogens liv, dens kraft, dens enorme humor, vidste hun, der fik ham til at klaske sig på lårene. Afbryd ikke, syntes han at sige til hende; tal ikke; bare sid. Og han læste videre. Hans læber trak sig. Det fyldte ham. Det gav ham styrke. Alle aftenens små irritationer og stik røg lige ud af hans hoved — hvor utåleligt kedeligt han fandt det at sidde stille, mens folk blev ved med at spise og drikke i det uendelige, hvor bidsk han havde været mod sin kone, hvor sårbar, hvor han havde taget sig nær af, at de sprang hen over hans bøger, som om de slet ikke fandtes. Men nu, følte han, var det pokkers ligegyldigt, hvem der nåede til Å (hvis tanken løb som et alfabet fra A til Å). Nogen ville nå derhen — hvis ikke han, så en anden. Forfatterens styrke og sunde fornuft, hans sans for de jævne og enkle ting, disse fiskere, den stakkels vanvittige gamle i Mucklebackits hytte (alt sammen i Scotts _Antikvaren_), fyldte ham med sådan en kraft, befriede ham for sådan noget, at han blev bevæget og triumferende og ikke kunne holde tårerne tilbage. Han løftede bogen en smule for at skjule ansigtet, lod tårerne falde, rystede på hovedet fra side til side og tabte sig selv fuldstændigt (bortset fra en tanke eller to om moral og om franske romaner kontra engelske, og om hvordan Scotts hænder var bundet, skønt hans syn måske var lige så sandt som det andet) — tabte alle sine egne bekymringer og nederlag i stakkels Steenies druknen og Mucklebackits sorg (det var Scott på sit bedste) og i den forbløffende fornøjelse og energi, det gav ham.

english: Well, let them do better than that, he thought, finishing the chapter. He had the feeling of having argued with someone and won. Whatever they said, they could not do better than that; and his own standing felt more secure. The lovers were rubbish, he thought, gathering the whole thing together in his mind once more. That part’s rubbish, this part’s first-rate, he thought, setting one piece against another. But he would have to read it again. The overall shape of it escaped him. He must keep his verdict open. So he went back to his other thought—if the young men didn’t care for this, then of course they didn’t care for him either. You mustn’t complain, Mr. Ramsay told himself, trying to smother his wish to complain to his wife that the young men didn’t admire him. But he had made up his mind: he would not bother her again. At this point he looked over at her, reading. She looked very peaceful as she read. He liked to think that the others had all gone off and left the two of them alone. Going to bed with a woman was not the whole of life, he thought, turning back to Scott and Balzac, to the English novel and the French.

Hvad de end sagde, kunne de ikke gøre det bedre end det; og hans egen stilling føltes mere sikker. De forelskede var noget makværk, tænkte han, mens han endnu en gang samlede det hele i sit sind. Den del er makværk, den del er førsteklasses, tænkte han og stillede det ene stykke op mod det andet. Men han måtte læse det igen. Den overordnede form undslap ham. Han måtte holde sin dom åben. Så han vendte tilbage til sin anden tanke — hvis de unge mænd ikke brød sig om dette, så brød de selvfølgelig heller ikke om ham. Man må ikke klage, sagde hr. Ramsay til sig selv og forsøgte at kvæle sit ønske om at klage over for sin kone over, at de unge mænd ikke beundrede ham. Men han havde besluttet sig: han ville ikke plage hende igen. Her så han over på hende, der læste. Hun så meget fredfyldt ud, mens hun læste. Han kunne lide at tænke, at de andre alle var gået og havde ladet de to alene. At gå i seng med en kvinde var ikke hele livet, tænkte han og vendte tilbage til Scott og Balzac, til den engelske roman og den franske.

english: As with your shadow I with these did play,
danish_before_fix: Med jeres skygge legede jeg med disse,
danish_after_fix: Med din skygge legede jeg med disse,

english: So, guided by some stray light from an uncovered star, or a wandering ship, or even the Lighthouse, with its pale footfall on stair and mat, the little breaths of air climbed the staircase and nosed around the bedroom doors. But here, surely, they must stop. Whatever else may perish and disappear, what lies here is steadfast. Here you might say to those sliding lights, those fumbling airs that breathe and bend over the bed itself: here you can neither touch nor destroy. At which, wearily, ghostlike, as if they had feather-light fingers and the light persistence of feathers, they would look once at the shut eyes and the loosely clasped fingers, and wearily fold their garments and disappear. And so, nosing, rubbing, they went to the window on the staircase, to the servants’ bedrooms, to the boxes in the attics; coming down again, they whitened the apples on the dining-room table, fumbled at the petals of the roses, tried the picture on the easel, brushed the mat and blew a little sand along the floor. At last, giving up, they all stopped together, gathered together, sighed together; all together they let out an aimless gust of lament, to which some door in the kitchen answered: it swung wide, let nothing in, and slammed shut.

Men her, helt sikkert, måtte de standse. Hvad end andet der måtte forgå og forsvinde, er det, der ligger her, urokkeligt. Her kunne man sige til de glidende lys, de famlende vinde, som åndede og bøjede sig over selve sengen: her kan I hverken røre eller ødelægge. Hvorpå de, trætte, spøgelsesagtige, som om de havde fingre let som fjer og fjerens spinkle udholdenhed, ville se én gang på de lukkede øjne og de løst knugede fingre og trætte folde deres klæder sammen og forsvinde. Og så, snusende, gnidende, gik de til vinduet på trappen, til tjenestefolkenes soveværelser, til kasserne på loftet; på vej ned igen gjorde de æblerne på spisestuebordet hvide, famlede ved rosernes kronblade, prøvede billedet på staffeliet, strøg over måtten og blæste lidt sand hen ad gulvet. Til sidst, da de opgav, standsede de alle sammen, samlede sig, sukkede sammen; alle sammen lod de et formålsløst vindstød af klage undslippe, som en dør i køkkenet svarede på: den svingede vidt op, lod intet komme ind og smækkede i.

english: So, with the house empty and the doors locked and the mattresses rolled up, those stray breaths of air, the advance guard of great armies, blustered in, brushed the bare boards, nibbled and fanned, and met nothing in bedroom or drawing room that fully resisted them—only hangings that flapped, wood that creaked, the bare legs of tables, saucepans and china already furred, tarnished, cracked. What people had shed and left behind—a pair of shoes, a shooting cap, some faded skirts and coats in the wardrobes—these alone kept the human shape, and in the emptiness showed how once they had been filled and brought to life; how once hands had been busy with hooks and buttons; how once the looking-glass had held a face, had held a hollowed-out world in which a figure turned, a hand flashed, the door opened, and in came children rushing and tumbling, and went out again. Now, day after day, the light turned its clear image on the opposite wall, like a flower reflected in water. Only the shadows of the trees, tossing in the wind, bowed low on the wall and for a moment darkened the pool in which the light reflected itself; or birds, flying past, made a soft spot flutter slowly across the bedroom floor.

Hvad folk havde smidt af sig og lagt tilbage — et par sko, en jagthue, nogle falmede skørter og frakker i klædeskabene — alene det bevarede den menneskelige skikkelse og viste i tomheden, hvordan det engang havde været fyldt og bragt til live; hvordan hænder engang havde været travlt optaget af hægter og knapper; hvordan spejlet engang havde rummet et ansigt, havde rummet en udhulet verden, hvori en skikkelse vendte sig, en hånd blinkede, døren åbnedes, og børn kom styrtende og væltende ind og gik ud igen. Nu kastede lyset dag efter dag sit klare billede på den modsatte væg som en blomst, der spejler sig i vand. Kun skyggerne af træerne, der slingrede i vinden, bukkede dybt på væggen og mørknede et øjeblik den dam, hvori lyset spejlede sig; eller fugle, der fløj forbi, fik en blød plet til at flagre langsomt hen over soveværelsets gulv.

english: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that asked to be spared the scorn and anger of the world—she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. Rubbing the glass of the long mirror and leering sideways at her swaying figure, she let a sound come from her lips—something that had perhaps been cheerful on the stage twenty years before, had been hummed and danced to, but now, coming from this toothless, bonneted caretaker, was robbed of meaning. It was like the voice of witlessness, of humor, of persistence itself, trodden down but springing up again; so that as she lurched along, dusting, wiping, she seemed to be saying how it was all one long sorrow and trouble, how it was getting up and going to bed again, and getting things out and putting them away again. It had not been easy or cozy, this world she had known for close on seventy years. She was bowed down with weariness. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? But she hobbled to her feet again, pulled herself up, and again, with her sidelong leer that slipped and turned aside even from her own face and her own sorrows, stood and gaped in the glass, smiling at nothing, and began again the old amble and hobble, taking up mats, putting down china, looking sideways in the glass—as if, after all, she had her consolations; as if some incorrigible hope really did twine itself around her dirge. There must have been visions of joy at the washtub, say, with her children (though two had been born out of wedlock and one had deserted her), or at the pub, drinking, or turning over odds and ends in her drawers. There must have been some break in the dark, some channel in the depths of obscurity through which enough light came to twist her face into a grin in the glass, and make her, turning to her work again, mumble out the old music-hall song. Meanwhile the mystics, the visionaries, walked the beach, stirred a puddle, looked at a stone, and asked themselves, “What am I?” “What is this?”—and suddenly an answer was granted them (what it was they could not say), so that they were warm in the frost and had comfort in the desert. But Mrs. McNab went on drinking and gossiping as before.
danish_before_fix: Mens hun slingrede af sted (for hun rullede som et skib på havet) og skelede (for hendes øjne faldt aldrig lige på noget, men kun med et sideblik, der bad om at blive skånet for verdens hån og vrede — hun var enfoldig, det vidste hun), mens hun greb fat i gelænderet og hev sig op ad trappen og rullede fra rum til rum, sang hun. Mens hun gnubbede glasset i det lange spejl og skelede sidelæns til sin vaklende skikkelse, lod hun en lyd komme fra sine læber — noget, der måske havde været muntert på scenen tyve år før, var blevet nynnet og danset til, men nu, når det kom fra denne tandløse, huebærende vicevært, var berøvet al mening. Det var som enfoldighedens, humorens, selve udholdenhedens stemme, nedtrampet, men skydende op igen; så at hun, mens hun slingrede af sted og støvede af og tørrede, syntes at sige, hvordan det hele var én lang sorg og møje, hvordan det var at stå op og gå i seng igen og tage ting frem og lægge dem på plads igen. Det havde ikke været let eller hyggeligt, denne verden hun havde kendt i næsten halvfjerds år. Hun var bøjet af træthed. Hvor længe, spurgte hun, mens hun knirkede og stønnede på knæ under sengen og støvede gulvbrædderne af, hvor længe skal det blive ved? Men hun humpede op på benene igen, trak sig op og stod atter med sit skelende sideblik, der gled og vendte sig bort selv fra hendes eget ansigt og hendes egne sorger, og gloede i spejlet, smilende til ingenting, og begyndte påny det gamle slæbende humpetrav, tog måtter op, stillede porcelæn på plads, så sidelæns i spejlet — som om hun trods alt havde sine trøster; som om et uforbederligt håb virkelig snoede sig om hendes klagesang. Der må have været glædesbilleder ved vaskebaljen, for eksempel, med hendes børn (skønt to var født uden for ægteskab, og én havde forladt hende), eller på kroen, når hun drak, eller når hun rodede i det løse i sine skuffer. Der må have været et brud i mørket, en kanal i dybet af tilsløring, gennem hvilken lys nok kom til at fortrække hendes ansigt til et grin i spejlet og få hende til, mens hun vendte sig mod sit arbejde igen, at mumle den gamle varietésang. Imens vandrede mystikerne, de synske, på stranden, rørte i en vandpyt, så på en sten og spurgte sig selv: »Hvad er jeg?« »Hvad er dette?« — og pludselig blev dem givet et svar (hvad det var, kunne de ikke sige), så de var varme i frosten og havde trøst i ørkenen. Men fru McNab blev ved med at drikke og sladre som før.

english: As summer drew near and the evenings lengthened, the wakeful and the hopeful who walked the beach and stirred the pools began to have the strangest imaginings: of flesh turned into atoms that drove before the wind, of stars flashing in their hearts, of cliff, sea, cloud and sky gathered together on purpose so that, out there, they might assemble the scattered pieces of the vision within. In those mirrors, the minds of men—in those pools of uneasy water, where clouds are always turning and shadows forming—dreams persisted. Every gull, flower, tree, man and woman, even the white earth itself, seemed to declare (though, if you questioned it, it would at once take the words back) that good triumphs, that happiness prevails, that order rules; and it was impossible to resist this strange hint. It was just as impossible to resist the extraordinary urge to roam this way and that in search of some absolute good, some crystal of intensity, far removed from familiar pleasures and known virtues—something alien to the business of domestic life, single, hard, bright, like a diamond in the sand, that would make its owner safe. Spring, meanwhile, had grown gentler and more yielding. With her bees humming and her gnats dancing, she drew her cloak around her, veiled her eyes and turned her head aside, and among the passing shadows and small gusts of rain she seemed to have taken on some knowledge of human sorrow.
danish_before_fix: Da sommeren nærmede sig, og aftenerne blev længere, begyndte de vågne og de håbefulde, som gik på stranden og rørte i vandpytterne, at få de sælsomste forestillinger: om kød, forvandlet til atomer, der drev for vinden, om stjerner, der lynede i deres hjerter, om klippe, hav, sky og himmel, samlet med vilje, så de derude kunne sætte de spredte stykker af synet indeni sammen. I de spejle, menneskenes sind — i de pytter af urolig vand, hvor skyer altid vender sig og skygger formes — blev drømmene ved. Hver måge, blomst, træ, mand og kvinde, selv den hvide jord, syntes at forkynde (skønt den straks ville tage ordene tilbage, hvis man spurgte den ud), at det gode sejrer, at lykken råder, at ordenen hersker; og det var umuligt at modstå dette sælsomme vink. Det var ligeså umuligt at modstå den ualmindelige trang til at strejfe hid og did på jagt efter noget absolut godt, en krystal af intensitet, langt fjernet fra velkendte fornøjelser og kendte dyder — noget fremmed for husholdningens gøremål, enkelt, hårdt, klart, som en diamant i sandet, der ville gøre sin ejer tryg. Foråret var imens blevet mildere og mere eftergivende. Med sine summende bier og dansende myg trak hun kappen om sig, sløret sine øjne og vendte hovedet bort, og blandt de forbipasserende skygger og de små regnbyger syntes hun at have fået nogen kundskab om menneskelig sorg.

english: Yet however deeply the house might slumber and sleep, later that summer ominous sounds reached it, like hammer blows falling in a slow rhythm, muffled on felt. Their repeated shocks loosened the shawl further still and cracked the teacups. Every so often a glass tinkled in the cupboard, as though some giant voice had screamed so loud in its agony that even the tumblers standing inside a cupboard shook too. Then silence fell once more. And then, night after night—and sometimes in the full light of noon, when the roses were bright and the light printed its shape plainly on the wall—there seemed to drop into this silence, this indifference, this wholeness, the thud of something falling.

Deres gentagne stød løsnede sjalet endnu mere og fik tekopperne til at revne. Nu og da klirrede et glas i skabet, som om en kæmpestemme havde skreget så højt i sin kval, at selv glassene, der stod inde i et skab, rystede med. Så faldt stilheden på ny. Og så, nat efter nat — og somme tider i fuldt middagslys, når rosenerne var klare, og lyset trykte sin form tydeligt på væggen — syntes der at falde ind i denne stilhed, denne ligegyldighed, denne helhed, dunket af noget, der faldt.

english: But what was the good of repeating it again and again? Why keep straining after a feeling she simply didn’t have? There was something like blasphemy in doing that. It was all dry: all shriveled: all used up. They should never have invited her; she should never have come. At forty-four you can’t afford to waste your time, she thought. She hated playing at painting. A brush was the one reliable thing in a world of conflict, ruin and chaos—you had no business playing with it, even knowingly; the idea disgusted her. But he forced her to. You won’t lay a finger on that canvas, he seemed to say as he bore down on her, until you’ve given me what I want from you. And here he was, right beside her again, greedy and distraught. Well, thought Lily despairingly, letting her right hand sink to her side, then it would be easier just to get it over with. Surely she could copy from memory the glow, the rapture, the self-surrender she had seen on the faces of so many women (on Mrs. Ramsay’s, for one) when, on an occasion like this, they would blaze up—she could recall the look on Mrs. Ramsay’s face—into a transport of sympathy, of delight in their reward. Why they felt it she could not tell, but plainly it gave them the most perfect bliss that human nature was capable of. Here he was, come to a stop beside her. She would give him what she could.
danish_before_fix: Men hvad nyttede det at gentage det igen og igen? Hvorfor blive ved med at anstrenge sig for en følelse, hun simpelthen ikke havde? Der var noget i retning af blasfemi i at gøre det. Det var alt sammen tørt: alt sammen skrumpet: alt sammen brugt op. De skulle aldrig have inviteret hende; hun skulle aldrig være kommet. Når man er fireogfyrre, har man ikke råd til at spilde sin tid, tænkte hun. Hun hadede at lege maler. En pensel var det eneste pålidelige i en verden af strid, ruin og kaos — man havde ingen ret til at lege med den, selv ikke med vidende vilje; tanken væmmedes hun ved. Men han tvang hende til det. Du lægger ikke en finger på det lærred, syntes han at sige, mens han bøjede ned over hende, før du har givet mig, hvad jeg vil have af dig. Og dér var han, lige ved siden af hende igen, grådig og fortvivlet. Nå, tænkte Lily håbløst og lod sin højre hånd sænke sig ned langs siden, så var det lettere bare at få det overstået. Hun kunne vel kopiere fra erindringen gløden, henrykkelsen, selvhengivelsen, hun havde set i så mange kvinders ansigter (i fru Ramsays, for eksempel), når de ved en lejlighed som denne ville flamme op — hun kunne genkalde sig udtrykket i fru Ramsays ansigt — i en vældig medfølelse, i glæde over deres belønning. Hvorfor de følte det, kunne hun ikke sige, men det gav dem åbenbart den fuldkomneste lyksalighed, den menneskelige natur var i stand til. Her var han, standset ved siden af hende. Hun ville give ham, hvad hun kunne.
danish_after_fix: Men hvad nyttede det at gentage det igen og igen? Hvorfor blive ved med at anstrenge sig for en følelse, hun simpelthen ikke havde? Der var noget i retning af blasfemi i at gøre det. Det var alt sammen tørt: alt sammen skrumpet: alt sammen brugt op. De skulle aldrig have inviteret hende; hun skulle aldrig være kommet. Når man er fireogfyrre, har man ikke råd til at spilde sin tid, tænkte hun. Hun hadede at lege maler. En pensel var det eneste pålidelige i en verden af strid, ruin og kaos — man havde ingen ret til at lege med den, selv ikke med vidende vilje; tanken væmmede hende. Men han tvang hende til det. Du lægger ikke en finger på det lærred, syntes han at sige, mens han bøjede ned over hende, før du har givet mig, hvad jeg vil have af dig. Og dér var han, lige ved siden af hende igen, grådig og fortvivlet. Nå, tænkte Lily håbløst og lod sin højre hånd sænke sig ned langs siden, så var det lettere bare at få det overstået. Hun kunne vel kopiere fra erindringen gløden, henrykkelsen, selvhengivelsen, hun havde set i så mange kvinders ansigter (i fru Ramsays, for eksempel), når de ved en lejlighed som denne ville flamme op — hun kunne genkalde sig udtrykket i fru Ramsays ansigt — i en vældig medfølelse, i glæde over deres belønning. Hvorfor de følte det, kunne hun ikke sige, men det gav dem åbenbart den fuldkomneste lyksalighed, den menneskelige natur var i stand til. Her var han, standset ved siden af hende. Hun ville give ham, hvad hun kunne.

english: “Trips like this,” said Mr. Ramsay, scraping the ground with the toe of his boot, “are very painful.” Still Lily said nothing. (She is a block of wood, she is a stone, he said to himself.) “They are very exhausting,” he said, looking at his beautiful hands with a sickly look that turned her stomach (he was acting, she felt; this great man was making a drama of himself). It was horrible, it was indecent. Would they never come? she asked herself, for she could not bear this enormous weight of sorrow, could not hold up these heavy drapes of grief (he had taken on a pose of extreme frailty; he even tottered a little as he stood there) a moment longer.
danish_before_fix: »Ture som denne,« sagde hr. Ramsay og skrabede i jorden med tåen af sin støvle, »er meget smertefulde.« Stadig sagde Lily intet. (Hun er en træklods, hun er en sten, sagde han til sig selv.) »De er meget udmattende,« sagde han og så på sine smukke hænder med et sygeligt udtryk, der vendte hendes mave (han spillede teater, følte hun; denne store mand lavede et drama ud af sig selv). Det var forfærdeligt, det var uanstændigt. Ville de aldrig komme? spurgte hun sig selv, for hun kunne ikke bære denne enorme tyngde af sorg, kunne ikke holde disse tunge draperier af kummer oppe (han havde taget en pose af ekstrem skrøbelighed på; han vaklede endda lidt, som han stod der) et øjeblik længere.

Det var forfærdeligt, det var uanstændigt. Ville de aldrig komme? spurgte hun sig selv, for hun kunne ikke bære denne enorme tyngde af sorg, kunne ikke holde disse tunge draperier af kummer oppe (han havde taget en positur af ekstrem skrøbelighed på; han vaklede endda lidt, som han stod der) et øjeblik længere.

english: But why did they have to come like _that_? She could not help feeling annoyed with them. They might have come more cheerfully; they might have given him what she, now that they were leaving, would have no chance to give him. For she felt a sudden emptiness, a frustration. Her feeling had come too late. There it was, ready, but he no longer needed it. He had turned into a very distinguished elderly man who had no need of her whatsoever. She felt snubbed. He slung a knapsack over his shoulders. He handed out the parcels—there were a number of them, badly tied, in brown paper. He sent Cam for a cloak. He looked every inch a leader getting ready for an expedition. Then, wheeling around, he led the way down the path with his firm military step, in those wonderful boots, carrying brown paper parcels, his children following him. They looked, she thought, as if fate had given them over to some stern undertaking, and they went to meet it, still young enough to be drawn along obediently in their father’s wake, but with a paleness in their eyes that made her feel they were silently suffering something beyond their years. So they passed the edge of the lawn, and it seemed to Lily that she was watching a procession go by, drawn on by some pressure of shared feeling which made it—faltering and flagging as it was—a little company bound together, and strangely impressive to her. Politely, but very distantly, Mr. Ramsay raised his hand and saluted her as they passed.
danish_before_fix: Men hvorfor skulle de komme på _den_ måde? Hun kunne ikke lade være med at føle sig irriteret på dem. De kunne have været mere muntre; de kunne have givet ham det, hun, nu da de var på vej af sted, ikke ville få chancen for at give ham. For hun følte en pludselig tomhed, en frustration. Hendes følelse var kommet for sent. Dér var den, parat, men han trængte ikke længere til den. Han var blevet til en meget fornem ældre mand, der slet ikke havde brug for hende. Hun følte sig afvist. Han slyngede en rygsæk over skuldrene. Han uddelte pakkerne — der var en del af dem, dårligt bundet ind i brunt papir. Han sendte Cam efter en kappe. Han så ud som en leder fra top til tå, der gjorde sig klar til en ekspedition. Så, vendt brat om, gik han i spidsen ned ad stien med sit faste, militære skridt, i de vidunderlige støvler, med brune papirpakker i hænderne og børnene efter sig. De så ud, tænkte hun, som om skæbnen havde overgivet dem til en streng opgave, og de gik den i møde, endnu unge nok til at lade sig trække lydigt med i deres fars kølvand, men med en bleghed i øjnene, der fik hende til at føle, at de i stilhed led noget, der lå hinsides deres år. Så de passerede kanten af plænen, og det forekom Lily, at hun så en procession gå forbi, draget frem af et pres af fælles følelse, der gjorde den — vaklende og slappende som den var — til et lille selskab, bundet sammen og besynderligt imponerende for hende. Høfligt, men meget fjernt løftede hr. Ramsay hånden og hilste hende, idet de gik forbi.
